scientific_name: Magnaporthe oryzae (Syn: P. grisea, Magnaporthe grisea)
content: Rice blast is caused by the fungus Magnaporthe oryzae (Syn: P. grisea, Magnaporthe grisea).

growth_stage: seedling to late tillering and ear heading stage
scientific_name: Magnaporthe oryzae (Syn: P. grisea, Magnaporthe grisea)
content: The fungus attacks the crop at all stages of crop growth from seedling to late tillering and ear heading stage. Symptoms appear on leaves, nodes, rachis, and glumes.

scientific_name: Magnaporthe oryzae (Syn: P. grisea, Magnaporthe grisea)
content: On the leaves, lesions appear as small bluish green flecks. Under moist weather, lesions enlarge to form characteristic spindle shaped spots with grey centre and dark brown margin. Spots coalesce as the disease progresses, large areas of leaves dry up and wither, and spots also appear on sheath. Severely infected nursery and field appear as burnt. The size and shape of spots vary on different rice varieties.

scientific_name: Magnaporthe oryzae (Syn: P. grisea, Magnaporthe grisea)
content: Black lesions appear on nodes girdling them. Affected nodes may break up and all plant parts above the infected nodes may die. Nodal infection causes the culm to break at the infected area.

scientific_name: Magnaporthe oryzae (Syn: P. grisea, Magnaporthe grisea)
content: Inter nodal infection occurs at the base of the plant which causes white panicles similar to that induced by yellow stem borer or water deficit.

scientific_name: Magnaporthe oryzae (Syn: P. grisea, Magnaporthe grisea)
content: Lesions on the neck are grayish brown and cause the girdling of the neck and the panicle to fall over. If neck infection occurs before the milky stage, no grain is formed; if infection occurs later, grains of poor quality are formed. Lesions on the branches of panicles and on spikelet pedicels are brown to dark brown.

disease: Brown Spot or Sesame leaf spot
content: Brown Spot or Sesame leaf spot causal organism is Helminthosporium oryzae (Sexual stage: Cochliobolus miyabeanus).

disease: Brown Spot or Sesame leaf spot
content: The fungus attacks the crop from seedling to milky stage in main field.

disease: Brown Spot or Sesame leaf spot
content: Symptoms appear as minute spots on the coleoptile, leaf blade, leaf sheath, and glume, being most prominent on the leaf blade and glumes. The spots become cylindrical or oval, dark brown with yellow halo.

disease: Brown Spot or Sesame leaf spot
content: Several spots coalesce and the leaf dries up. The seedlings die and affected nurseries can be often recognised from a distance by scorched appearance.

disease: Brown Spot or Sesame leaf spot
content: Dark brown or black spots also appear on glumes leading to grain discoloration.

disease: Brown Spot or Sesame leaf spot
content: Brown spot causes failure of seed germination, seedling mortality and reduces the grain quality and weight.

Bacterial blight syndrome exhibits three types of symptoms: leaf blight, kresek (the seedling blight or wilt phase) and the pale-yellow leaf. Seedlings in the nursery show circular, yellow spots in the margin, that enlarge, coalesce leading to drying of foliage. 'Kresek' symptom is seen in seedlings, 1-2 weeks after transplanting, where bacteria enter through the cut wounds in the leaf tips, become systemic and cause death of the entire seedling.

In grown up plants, water-soaked, translucent lesions appear near the leaf margin. The lesions enlarge both in length and width with a wavy margin and turn straw yellow within a few days, covering the entire leaf. As the disease advances, the lesions cover the entire lamina which turns white or straw coloured. Milky or opaque dew drops containing bacterial masses are formed on young lesions in the early morning and dry up on the surface leaving a white encrustation. Affected grains have discoloured spots.
If the cut end of an infected leaf is dipped in water, it becomes turbid because of bacterial ooze.

The bacterium is aerobic, gram negative, non-spore forming, rod-shaped with size ranging from 1-2 x 0.8-1.0 µm with monotrichous polar flagellum. Bacterial colonies are circular, convex with entire margins, whitish yellow to straw yellow colored, and opaque.

Favourable conditions for bacterial leaf blight include clipping of the tip of the seedling at the time of transplanting, heavy rain, heavy dew, flooding, deep irrigation water, severe wind, temperature of 25-30 °C, and application of excessive nitrogen, especially late top dressing.

scientific_name: Rice tungro bacilliform virus (RTBV) and Rice tungro spherical virus (RTSV)
content: Rice tungro virus is caused by Rice tungro bacilliform virus (RTBV) and Rice tungro spherical virus (RTSV). It is vectored by the Green leafhopper, Nephotettix virescens.

growth_stage: all growth stages, specifically vegetative stage
scientific_name: Rice tungro bacilliform virus (RTBV) and Rice tungro spherical virus (RTSV)
content: Plants affected by tungro exhibit stunting and reduced tillering. Leaves become yellow or orange-yellow, and may have rust-colored spots. Yellowing starts from the tip of the leaf and may extend to the lower part of the leaf blade. The third leaf from the top of most infected plants is taller than other leaves. Young leaves are often mottled with pale green to whitish interveinal stripes, and old leaves may have rusty streaks of various sizes. Flowering is delayed, and panicles are small and not completely exerted. Most panicles are sterile or have partially filled grains. The plants may be killed if infected early. Tungro virus disease affects all growth stages of the rice plant, specifically high at vegetative stage.

scientific_name: Rice tungro bacilliform virus (RTBV) and Rice tungro spherical virus (RTSV)
content: Tungro infected plants can be chemically identified by Iodine Test: Collect leaf samples at 6 a.m. The top 10 cm portion of the leaf is immersed in a solution containing 2 g of iodine and 6 g of potassium iodide in 100 ml of water for 15 minutes, or 10 ml of tincture of iodine + 140 ml of water for one hour. Washed in water for detection. Tungro infected leaves develop dark blue streaks.

growth_stage: all growth stages, specifically vegetative stage
scientific_name: Rice tungro bacilliform virus (RTBV) and Rice tungro spherical virus (RTSV)
content: Factors favouring disease development include: Presence of the virus sources; Presence of the vector; Age and susceptibility of host plants; Synchronization of the three above factors; and all growth stages of rice plant specifically the vegetative stage.
Causal organism of Sheath Rot is Sarocladium oryzae (Syn : Acrocylindrium oryzae).

Initial symptoms are noticed only on the upper most leaf sheath enclosing young panicles. The flag leaf sheath shows oblong or irregular greyish brown spots (brown discolouration of boot leaf sheath). They enlarge and develop grey centre and brown margins covering major portions of the leaf sheath. The young panicles may remain within the sheath or emerge partially. The panicles rot and abundant whitish powdery fungal growth is formed inside the leaf sheath.
The fungus produces whitish, sparsely branched, septate mycelium. Conidia are hyaline, smooth, single celled and cylindrical in shape.

pest: leaf folder, brown plant hopper, mites
content: Favourable conditions include closer planting, high doses of nitrogen, high humidity, and temperature around 25-30 C. Injuries made by leaf folder, brown plant hopper and mites increase infection.
Mainly spreads through air-borne conidia and also seed-borne.
Grow moderately resistant varieties viz., CO 55 and ADT 59.
Treat the seeds with Thiram at 4 g/kg or Bacillus subtilis (TNAU) @ 10g/kg of seed.
Soil application of gypsum (200 kg/ac) in two splits.
Application of NSKE 5% or neem oil 3 % or Ipomoea or prosopis leaf powder extract 10 Kg/ac. First spray at boot leaf stage and second 15 days later.
Foliar spray with thiophanate methyl 70% WP 500 gm acre or soil application of hexaconazole 0.5% GR 4 kg per acre at tillering stage.

growth_stage: tillering to heading stage, grain filling
content: The fungus affects the crop from tillering to heading stage, and older plants are highly susceptible. Initial symptoms appear on leaf sheaths near the water level as oval, elliptical, or irregular greenish-grey spots. As spots enlarge, the centre turns greyish-white with an irregular blackish-brown or purple-brown border. Lesions coalesce on upper plant parts, covering entire tillers from the waterline to the flag leaf. Several large lesions can kill the whole leaf, and in severe cases all leaves are blighted, extending to inner sheaths and causing death of the entire plant. Heavy infection in early heading and grain-filling stages results in poorly filled grains, especially in the lower panicle.
The fungus produces septate mycelium which are hyaline when young and yellowish brown when old. It produces a large number of spherical brown sclerotia.

Favourable conditions for disease development include: presence of sclerotia or infection bodies floating on water; presence of sclerotia in the soil; relative humidity from 96 to 100%; temperature from 28 to 32 °C; high levels of nitrogen fertilizer; high seeding rate or close plant spacing; and frequent rain.
The pathogen survives as sclerotia or mycelium in dry soil for about 20 months and in moist soil for 5 to 8 months. Sclerotia spread via irrigation water. The fungus has a wide host range.
Grow moderately resistant varieties including ADT 56, ADT 57, ADT 59, and KKM 1.
Apply organic amendments such as neem cake @ 60 kg/ac or FYM at 5 tonnes/ha. Avoid flow of irrigation water from infected fields to healthy fields. Perform deep ploughing in summer and burn stubbles.
Spray Carbendazim @ 100 g/ac.

growth_stage: 30 days after transplanting, boot leaf stage
content: Apply B. subtilis (TNAU) to the soil @ 1 kg/ac mixed with 20 kg of FYM/sand 30 days after transplanting. Apply foliar spray at 0.2% (400 g/ac) at boot leaf stage and repeat 10 days later.

The fungus transforms individual ovaries/grains into greenish spore balls of velvety appearance. Few to several spikelets in a panicle are affected. Initially smut balls are yellow and turn greenish black at maturity.

Sclerotia present in soil germinate and produce ascospores, serving as the primary source of inoculum. Chlamydospores are formed in infected grains as spore balls which are spherical to elliptical, warty, and olivaceous. Smut spores are air borne and responsible for secondary spread.
Rainfall and cloudy weather during flowering and maturity, along with high soil nitrogen, are favourable conditions for the disease.
Grow moderately resistant varieties viz., CO 59.

Use disease-free seeds selected from a healthy crop. Adopt split application of nitrogen and avoid excess application of nitrogenous fertilizer. Remove and properly dispose of infected plant debris, and destroy straw and stubble from infected plants. Early planted crop has less smut balls than late planted crop. At harvest time, remove and destroy diseased plants to prevent sclerotia from falling into the field and reducing primary inoculum for the next crop. Keep field bunds and irrigation channels clean to eliminate alternate hosts.
Perform seed treatment with carbendazim at 2.0 g/kg of seeds.
At booting and pre-flowering stages, spray copper hydroxide 77 WP at 800 g/acre or copper hydroxide 53.8% DF at 600 ml/acre or thifluzamide 15% + difenoconazole 20% SC at 100 ml per acre.

Fine translucent streaks are formed on the veins and the lesions enlarge lengthwise and infect larger veins and turn brown. On the surface of the lesions, bacterial ooze comes out and forms small yellow band-like exudates under humid conditions. In severe cases the leaves dry up.

The bacterium is aerobic, gram negative, non spore forming, rod with size ranging from 1-2 x 0.8-1.0 µm with monotrichous polar flagellum. Bacterial colonies are circular, convex with entire margins, whitish yellow to straw yellow colored and opaque.

Favourable conditions include clipping of tip of the seedling at the time of transplanting, heavy rain, heavy dew, flooding, deep irrigation water, severe wind, temperature of 25-30 °C, and application of excessive nitrogen, especially late top dressing.
It is transmitted through seeds and infected stubbles to the next planting season. The pathogen spreads through irrigation water and also through rain storms.

Cultural management includes: burn the stubbles, use optimum dose of fertilizers, avoid clipping of tip of seedling at the time of transplanting, avoid flooded conditions, and remove weed hosts periodically.

Seed treatment: Soaking of seeds in streptomycin sulphate 90% and tetracycline 10% SP @ 40 ppm for 12 hours or seedling root dipping @ 40 ppm for 30 minutes. Foliar spray in the main field @ 100-150 ppm; repeat the spray after 15 days, if required.

Infected plants are several inches taller than normal plants in seedbed and field. Plants are thin with yellowish green leaves and pale green flag leaves. Drying of seedlings occurs at early tillering. Late infection causes reduced tillering and drying leaves. Surviving plants at maturity have partially filled grains, sterile or empty grains. In the seedbed, infected seedlings with lesions on roots will die, which may die before or after transplanting.

The fungus produces both macro and microconidia. Microconidia are hyaline, single celled and oval. Macroconidia are slightly sickle shaped, and two to five celled. The fungus produces the phytotoxin, fusaric acid, which is non-host specific.
The fungus is externally seed-borne.
Treat the seeds with Thiram or Captan or Carbendazim at 2 g/kg.

The infected plants are stunted and have yellowish green to whitish green leaves. There is excessive tillering and leaves become soft and droop slightly. Root growth is also reduced significantly. Chlorosis occurs on the leaves occasionally even spreading to the leaf sheaths. Streaks may also form parallel to the leaf veins. If plants are infected early they usually die before maturity and even if they do survive no panicles are produced or only a small number with no grains.
Phytoplasma is transmitted by Nephotettix virescens and N. nigropictus with a latent period of 25-30 days. It survives on several grass weeds.
Rice varieties like IR62 and IR64 are resistant to the disease.

Deep ploughing during summer and burning of stubbles. The management practices followed for Rice Tungro Disease (RTD) may be adopted for this disease also. Avoiding early planted rice will prevent an increase in vector density and proportion of virus acquired vectors. Planting fallow rice fields with non vector hosts, ploughing fallow paddy fields and late-planting, synchronous planting or avoiding an overlap of early and late planted rice crops. Remove weed hosts periodically. Crop rotation.

Vector control with any one of the following insecticides: Thiamethoxam 25 WDG 40g/acre (or) Imidacloprid 17.8 SL 40 ml/acre spray at 15 and 30 days after transplanting. The vegetation on the bunds should also be sprayed with the insecticides.

Diseased hills are severely stunted with excessive tillering and a very upright growth habit, showing a grassy and rosette appearance. Leaves are short, narrow, yellowish-green with numerous small rusty spots or patches forming blotches. Leaves retain green coloration after application of sufficient nitrogenous fertilizers. Infected plants usually survive until maturity but produce no panicles. Symptoms develop 10-20 days after infection.

Rice grassy stunt virus (RGSV) is a member of the Tenuiviruses. It has fine filamentous particles that are 6-8 nm in diameter, with a nodal contour length of 950-1,350 nm. The particles have one capsid protein and the genome is composed of four single stranded RNA.

The virus exists in the vector and in the rice crop, and is transmitted by Brown plant hopper (Nilaparvata lugens) nymphs and adults where rice is grown year round. RGSV is generally endemic. Macropterous forms (long-winged adults) are more important in spreading the disease than short-winged forms. Insects feed on diseased plants for at least 30 minutes to pick up the virus, and higher infection is attained after prolonged inoculation feeding periods of up to 24 hours. The availability of the vector encourages disease damage.

Avoid close planting and provide 30 cm rogue spacing at every 2.5 to 3.0 m to reduce pest incidence. Plough and harrow the field to destroy stubbles right after harvest in order to eradicate other hosts.
Grow varieties released by IRRI that contain genes for BPH resistance, such as IR26, IR64, IR36, IR56, and IR72.
Apply any one of the following insecticides to control vector BPH: Phosalone 35 EC at 600 ml/acre, Acephate 75 SP at 250 ml/acre, or Chlorpyriphos 20 EC at 500 ml/acre.

scientific_name: Drechslera oryzae, D. rostratum, D.tetramera, Curvularia lunata, Trichoconis padwickii, Sarocladium oryzae, Alternaria tenuis, Fusarium moniliforme, Cladosporium herbarum, Epicoccum purpurascens, Cephalosporium sp., Phoma sp. and Nigrospora sp.
content: Causal organisms associated with discoloured grains include Drechslera oryzae, D. rostratum, D.tetramera, Curvularia lunata, Trichoconis padwickii, Sarocladium oryzae, Alternaria tenuis, Fusarium moniliforme, Cladosporium herbarum, Epicoccum purpurascens, Cephalosporium sp., Phoma sp. and Nigrospora sp.

scientific_name: Drechslera oryzae, D. rostratum, D.tetramera, Curvularia lunata, Trichoconis padwickii, Sarocladium oryzae, Alternaria tenuis, Fusarium moniliforme, Cladosporium herbarum, Epicoccum purpurascens, Cephalosporium sp., Phoma sp. and Nigrospora sp.
content: The grains may be infected by various organisms before or after harvesting causing discolouration, the extent of which varies according to season and locality. The infection may be external or internal causing discoloration of the glumes or kernels or both. Dark brown or black spots appear on the grains. The discolouration may be red, yellow, orange, pink or black, depending upon the organism involved and the degree of infection. This disease is responsible for quantitative and qualitative losses of grains.
High humidity and cloudy weather during heading stage are favourable conditions for grain discolouration.
The disease spreads mainly through air-borne conidia and the fungus survives as parasite and saprophyte in the infected grains, plant debris and also on other crop debris.
Pre and post-harvest measures should be taken into account for prevention of grain discolouration.
Seed treatment with Thiram at 4 g/kg or Bacillus subtilis (TNAU) @ 10g/kg.
Foliar spray of Neem oil @ 3 per cent at 50% flowering stage followed by second spray 10 days later.
Foliar spray with thiophanate methyl 70% WP or hexaconazole 4% + zineb 68% WP 400 gm per acre at 50 per cent flowering.

Rice is a crop of tropical climate, but is also grown successfully in humid to sub-humid regions under subtropical and temperate climate. Under high temperature, high humidity with sufficient rainfall and irrigation facilities, rice can be grown in any type of soil.

Rice is cultivated in almost all types of soils with varying productivity. Major soil groups include riverine alluvium, red-yellow, red loamy, hill and sub-montane, Terai, laterite, coastal alluvium, red sandy, mixed red and black, and medium and shallow black soils.

Tamil Nadu rice seasons: Navarai (sowing Dec - Jan, duration < 120 days); Sornavari (sowing Apr - May, duration < 120 days); Early Kar / Kar (sowing Apr – May / May - June, duration < 120 days); Kuruvai (sowing June - July, duration < 120 days); Early Samba (sowing July - Aug, duration 130 to 135 days); Samba (sowing August, duration 130 – 135 and > 150 days); Late Samba / Thaladi / Pishanam (sowing Sep - Oct, duration 130 - 135 days); Late Pishanam (sowing Sep - Oct, duration 130 - 135 days); Late Thaladi (sowing Oct - Nov, duration 115 - 120 days).

Rice cultivation systems in Tamil Nadu are grouped into: 1. Transplanted puddled lowland rice; 2. Direct seeded lowland rice (wet seeded in puddled soil, dry seeded in un-puddled soil under rainfed, semi-dry supplemental irrigation, or semi-dry canal irrigation); 3. Dry seeded upland rice (sloping/terraced land with high rainfall, e.g., limited area in Dharmapuri); 4. Deep water rice (pockets of Nagapattinam and Tiruvarur districts).

subtopic: wet nursery land area and seed rate
content: For transplanted puddled lowland rice, select 20 cents (800 m2) of nursery area near a water source to raise seedlings for 1 ha. Seed rate: > 30 kg for long duration, 40 kg for medium duration, 60 kg for short duration varieties, and 20 kg for hybrids.

Treat seeds in Carbendazim or Pyroquilon or Tricyclozole solution at 2 g/l of water for 1 kg of seeds. Soak for 10 hrs and drain excess water (protects up to 40 days from seedling diseases such as blast). For immediate sowing, keep soaked seed in dark covered with gunnies for 24 hrs for sprouting. Alternatively, treat with talc-based Pseudomonas fluorescens at 10 g/kg seed soaked in 1 liter water overnight, decant and sprout for 24 hrs. For biofertilizers, mix 3 packets (600 g/ha) Azospirillum and 3 packets (600 g/ha) Phosphobacteria or 6 packets (1200 g/ha) Azophos with water, soaking seeds overnight. Biocontrol agents and biofertilizers can be mixed together, but fungicides and biocontrol agents are incompatible.

subtopic: wet nursery seedbed formation and sowing
content: Mark plots of 2.5 m breadth with 30 cm wide channels all around. Bed length varies from 8 to 10 m according to soil and slope. Raise beds with puddled soil collected from channels and level the surface. Sow sprouted seeds uniformly on the seedbed with a thin film of water.

Drain water 18 to 24 hrs after sowing; avoid stagnation in any part of the seedbed. Saturate soil from 3rd to 5th day. From 5th day onwards, increase water depth to 1.5 cm depending on seedling height; thereafter maintain 2.5 cm depth of water.

Apply pre-emergence herbicide Pretilachlor + safener @ 0.3 kg/ha on 3rd or 4th day after sowing to control weeds in lowland nursery. Keep a thin film of water and allow it to disappear without draining.

Apply 1 tonne of fully decomposed FYM or compost to 20 cents nursery dry soil uniformly. For seedlings pulled at 20-25 days in less fertile soils, apply 40 kg DAP basally before last puddling (or 16 kg urea + 120 kg super phosphate). If seedlings are pulled after 25 days, apply DAP 10 days prior to pulling. In clayey soils prone to root snapping, apply 4 kg gypsum and 1 kg DAP per cent at 10 days after sowing.

Dry ploughed field with fine tilth and sandy/loamy soil is suitable. Nursery area is 20 cents. Form beds of 1 to 1.5 m width with channels; raised beds are ideal for clayey soils. Seed rate and treatment same as wet nursery. Dry sow seeds, cover with sand and finely powdered well-decomposed FYM, and irrigate to saturation. Optimum age for transplanting is the 4th leaf stage.

Plough land during summer to economize water. Flood the field 1-2 days before ploughing to soak. Maintain water depth at 2.5 cm at the time of puddling. Puddling and tractor-drawn cage wheel ploughing reduce percolation losses and water requirement by up to 20%.

For fluffy paddy soils: compact soil by passing a 400 kg stone roller or oil-drum filled with stones 8 times at 13-18% moisture level once in 3 years. For sodic soils (pH > 8.5): apply gypsum at 50% gypsum requirement, impound water, provide drainage for salt leaching, apply green leaf manure at 5 t/ha 10-15 days before transplanting, and spread 37.5 kg ZnSO4 mixed with sand (75 kg total) uniformly without incorporating. For saline soils (EC > 4 dS/m): provide 60 cm deep and 45 cm wide drainage channels, apply green leaf manure at 5 t/ha 10-15 days before transplanting, 25% extra nitrogen, and ZnSO4 @ 37.5 kg/ha. For acid soils: apply lime @ 2.5 t/ha before last ploughing for each crop up to the 5th crop based on soil test.

Optimum seedling age for transplanting is 18-22 days for short, 25-30 days for medium, and 35-40 days for long duration varieties (at 4th leaf stage; 3rd leaf stage can be pulled if thin film water management and leveling are maintained). Transplanting beyond 5th leaf stage leads to aged seedlings and yield loss.

Prepare a slurry with 5 packets (1000 g/ha) Azospirillum and 5 packets (1000 g/ha) Phosphobacteria (or 10 packets/2000 g/ha Azophos) in 40 liters of water. Dip the seedling root portion for 15-30 minutes before transplanting.

Planting density: In medium/low fertility soils: Short duration: 15x10 cm (66 hills/m2); Medium duration: 20x10 cm (50 hills/m2); Long duration: 20x15 cm (33 hills/m2). In high fertility soils: Short duration: 20x10 cm (50 hills/m2); Medium duration: 20x15 cm (33 hills/m2); Long duration: 20x20 cm (25 hills/m2). Plant 2-3 seedlings/hill for short duration and 2 seedlings/hill for medium and long duration varieties at shallow depth (3 cm). Line planting requires a minimum row spacing of 20 cm for rotary weeders. Gap filling should be completed between 7th and 10th DAT.

For aged seedlings (developed tillers/node elongation in nursery): follow spacing recommended for medium/low fertility soil, plant 1-2 seedlings per hill, avoid cluster planting, and enhance basal nitrogen application by 50% over recommended dose to encourage new tiller formation.

Apply 12.5 t FYM or compost or green leaf manure @ 6.25 t/ha. If green manure is grown in situ @ 20 kg/ha, incorporate to 15 cm depth using a green manure trampler or tractor. Press-mud or composted coir-pith can substitute green manure. When incorporating stubbles of previous crop, apply 22 kg urea/ha at first puddling (at least 10 days prior to planting) to compensate for N immobilization.

For dry season crop, broadcast 10 kg soil-based powdered blue green algae (BGA) flakes at 10 DAT and maintain a thin water film. For wet season crop, raise Azolla as dual crop by inoculating 250 kg/ha at 3-5 DAT and incorporate during weeding. Before transplanting, broadcast 10 packets (2000 g/ha) Azospirillum + 10 packets (2000 g/ha) Phosphobacteria (or 20 packets/4000 g/ha Azophos) mixed with 25 kg FYM and 25 kg soil, and Pseudomonas fluorescens (Pf 1) @ 2.5 kg/ha mixed with 50 kg FYM and 25 kg soil.

Blanket fertilizer recommendations: Short duration varieties (dry season): Cauvery delta & Coimbatore tract: 150:50:50 kg N:P2O5:K2O/ha; Other tracts: 120:40:40 kg N:P2O5:K2O/ha. Medium and long duration varieties (wet season): 150:50:50 kg N:P2O5:K2O/ha. Hybrid rice: 175:60:60 kg N:P2O5:K2O/ha. Low N responsive cultivars (e.g., Improved White Ponni): 75:50:50 kg N:P2O5:K2O/ha, with N applied in 3 splits at Active Tillering, Panicle Initiation, and Heading.

subtopic: split application and LCC based N management
content: Apply N and K in 4 equal splits at basal, tillering, panicle initiation, and heading stages. For LCC management, take weekly observations from 14 DAT (or 21 DAS in direct seeded) up to heading between 8-10 am using the fully opened 3rd leaf from top across 10 places. Critical LCC value is 3.0 for low N responsive cultivars (White Ponni) and 4.0 for other cultivars and hybrids. If 6 out of 10 observations fall below the critical value, apply 35 kg N/ha in dry season or 30 kg N/ha in wet season.

subtopic: phosphorus, zinc, gypsum, and foliar application
content: Apply P basally. Rock phosphate can be used with green manure; rock phosphate + SSP or DAP (75:25 or 50:50) is effective. Apply 25 kg ZnSO4 mixed with 50 kg dry sand just before transplanting (or 12.5 kg ZnSO4/ha if green manure or enriched FYM is applied). If Zn deficiency appears, spray 0.5% ZnSO4 + 1.0% urea at 15-day intervals. Apply 500 kg gypsum/ha at last ploughing. Foliar spray: 1% urea + 2% DAP + 1% KCl at panicle initiation and 10 days later.

Nitrogen deficiency: Stunted plants, lower leaves yellowing first, starting at leaf tip progressing along midrib; leaves turn brown and die in severe cases. Potassium deficiency: Bluish green young leaves, older leaves irregular with chlorotic and necrotic areas, poor grain formation, straw weakening/lodging. Magnesium deficiency: Chlorotic leaves with white tips. Iron toxicity: Brown spots on lower leaves starting at tips to base, turning green or orange-purple and spreading upwards. Zinc deficiency: Chlorotic lower leaves towards base; plants display a brown rusty appearance.

Blend urea with crushed neem seed/cake at 20% by weight (sieved through 2 mm sieve) and keep overnight before use; alternatively mix urea with gypsum (1:3 ratio) or urea + gypsum + neem cake (5:4:1 ratio). For coal-tar treated urea: dissolve 1 kg coal-tar (melted over low flame) in 1.5 L kerosene per 100 kg urea, mix thoroughly, and dry in shade; stores for a month and applied basally.

subtopic: weed control practices in transplanted rice
content: Use rotary weeder from 15 DAT at 10-day intervals. Apply pre-emergence herbicides on 3rd DAT mixed with 50 kg dry sand with a thin film of water (do not drain or add fresh irrigation for 2 days): Butachlor 1.25 kg/ha, Anilophos 0.4 kg/ha, or mixture of Butachlor 0.6 kg + 2,4-DEE 0.75 kg/ha, or Anilophos + 2,4-DEE ready-mix at 0.4 kg/ha, followed by hand weeding at 30-35 DAT. For post-emergence weed control, hand weed at 15 DAT, or spray 2,4-D sodium salt (Fernoxone 80% WP) @ 1.25 kg/ha in 625 L water at 3 weeks after transplanting or at 3-4 weed leaf stage.

Maintain 2 cm water at transplanting and up to 7 DAT. Thereafter, follow cyclic 5 cm submergence throughout crop period: irrigate 1 day after disappearance of ponded water in summer (3 days in winter for loamy soils; just before/immediately after disappearance in clayey soils in summer, 1-2 days in winter). Critical water requirement stages: panicle initiation, booting, heading, and flowering (do not deplete moisture below saturation). Stop irrigation 15 days ahead of harvest. Avoid continuous inundation (> 5 cm) during booting and maturity as it causes root decay and poor filling.

Drain water 7 to 10 days before expected harvest. Harvest when 80% of panicles turn straw colour and grains at base of panicle reach hard dough stage (clear and firm when dehusked). Thresh, winnow, and dry grains to 12% moisture level for storage (yield estimated at 14% moisture). Maturity can be hastened by 3-4 days by spraying 20% NaCl a week before harvest to escape monsoon rains.

Use 20-day-old seedlings of short duration varieties thrown into puddled leveled field without force (seedling requirement is ~20% more than line planting). Suitable for all seasons except Thaladi or heavy rain season. Saves 50% labor vs line planting and 35% vs random planting. Maintain thin film of water for 7-10 days after throwing.

Seed rate: 20 kg/ha. Nursery: apply DAP @ 2 kg/cent basally; sow sparsely at 1 kg/cent to obtain robust seedlings; apply 4 kg gypsum/cent 10 days before pulling if soil is heavy. Age of seedlings: 20 to 25 days. Spacing: 20x10 cm (50 hills/m2) or 25x10 cm (40 hills/m2). Plant 1 seedling/hill. Fertilizer: 175:60:60 kg N:P2O5:K2O/ha.

SRI is suited for dry season with assured irrigation. Seed rate: 7-8 kg/ha for 1 seedling/hill, 12-15 kg/ha for 2 seedlings/hill. Mat nursery: prepare 100 m2 nursery area for 1 ha on plastic sheets/gunnies; mix 70% soil + 20% decomposed organic manure + 10% rice hull with 1.5 kg DAP or 2 kg 17-17-17 fertilizer. Sow pre-germinated seeds (90-100 g/m2), cover with 5 mm soil, water with rose can. Transplant 15-day-old seedlings (1-2 per hill) within 30 minutes of lifting at 22.5 x 22.5 cm square spacing in well-leveled puddled field. Gap fill at 7-10 DAT. Irrigate only to moisten soil for first 10 days, then irrigate to 2.5 cm after hairline cracks appear until PI; increase to 5 cm depth 1 day after disappearance of ponded water after PI. Weeding using rotary/cono weeder at 7-10 day intervals from 10-15 DAT in both directions.

Damage symptoms: Laceration of tender leaves, sucking sap; yellow or silvery streaks on young seedling leaves; terminal leaf rolling and drying from tip to base in nursery and main field. Management: Sample by passing wet palm over foliage 12 times; if population exceeds 60 thrips or rolling in 10% seedlings is observed, spray nursery with Phosphamidon 40 SL @ 50 ml or Endosulfan 35 EC @ 80 ml.

Damage symptoms: Yellowing of leaves from tip downwards. Acts as vector for Rice tungro virus, rice yellow, and transitory yellowing. Management: Grow resistant varieties (IR 50, CR 1009, Co 46); apply neem cake @ 12.5 kg/20 cent nursery as basal dose; spray vegetation on bunds with insecticides; set up light traps.

Damage symptoms: Caterpillars feed on green tissues causing leaves to become whitish papery; construct tubular cases around tillers by cutting apical portions of leaves; tubular cases float on water. Management: Drain water; dislodge cases with running rope; in nursery, mix 100 ml kerosene in standing water and spray Endosulfan 35 EC @ 30 ml/8 cents; in field spray Endosulfan 35 EC @ 1000 ml/ha or Monocrotophos 36 WSC @ 500 ml/ha.

Damage symptoms: Brown egg mass near leaf tip; caterpillar bores into central shoot causing drying of central shoot ('dead heart') in seedlings/tillers, and dried whole panicle ('white ear') in grown-up plants. Management: Resistant varieties (Ratna, Jaya, TKM 6); avoid close planting and continuous water stagnation; pull and destroy affected tillers; install light traps; harvest at ground level; release egg parasitoid Trichogramma japonicum twice @ 5 cc/ha (followed by spray thrice @ 1000 ml/ha on 58, 65, 72 DAT); apply Bacillus thuringiensis var kurstaki and NSKE; spray Endosulfan 35 EC @ 1000 ml/ha, Quinalphos 25 EC @ 1000 ml/ha, Phosphamidon 40 SL @ 600 ml/ha, or Profenophos 50 EC @ 1000 ml/ha.

Damage symptoms: Larvae cut seedlings on a large scale giving a cattle-grazed appearance; feed gregariously and march from field to field. Management: Kerosenate water during irrigation; allow ducks into field; in nursery, drain water and spray Chlorpyriphos 20 EC @ 80 ml or Endosulfan 35 EC @ 80 ml in 20 L water for 8 cents.

Damage symptoms: Maggot feeds at base of growing shoot causing formation of a tube-like gall ('onion leaf' or 'silver-shoot'); infested tillers produce no panicles. Management: Early ploughing; resistant varieties (MDU 3, Shakthi, Vikram, Sureka); harvest crop and plough immediately; remove alternate hosts; plant early maturing varieties; apply optimum potash fertilizer; monitor with light traps.
Damage symptoms: Edges of leaves are fastened with webbing; backward rolling of leaves; caterpillar feeds from margin inwards.

Damage symptoms: Leaves fold longitudinally, larvae scrape green tissues turning them white and dry; scorched appearance in severe infestation. Management: Use resistant varieties (TNAU LFR 831311, Cauveri, Akash, TKM 6); clip affected leaves; keep bunds clean; avoid excessive N fertilizers; use light traps; release Trichogramma chilonis @ 1,25,000/ha thrice; spray NSKE 5%, Carbaryl 50 WP @ 1 kg/ha, or Chlorpyriphos 20 EC @ 1250 ml/ha.
Damage symptoms: Larva feeds on leaf blades causing irregular defoliation from margin or tip; yellow eye-like spot on each forewing.

Damage symptoms: Irregular feeding on seedlings and leaf blades, cutting of stems at panicle stage, completely defoliating plants leaving only midribs. Management: Expose eggs to birds by ploughing and trimming bunds; dust Malathion 5% @ 20 kg/ha.

Damage symptoms: Adults scrape chlorophyll causing white parallel streaks and white patches along long leaf axis; grubs mine into leaves creating blisters near leaf tips. Management: Destroy leaf tips containing blotch mines; manually collect and kill beetles using hand nets; spray Endosulfan 35 EC @ 1000 ml/ha.

Damage symptoms: Maggot feeds on tender tissue inside whorl, causing yellowish-white longitudinal marginal blotching with holes; leaves shrivel, plants are stunted, maturity delayed; drooping of young leaves near tip. Management: Grow early maturing varieties, apply optimum potash fertilizer, and spray Endosulfan 35 EC @ 1000 ml/ha.

Damage symptoms: Nymphs and adults suck sap at plant base above water level; plants dry up showing scorched 'hopper burn' appearance in circular patches with lodging; transmits grassy stunt, ragged stunt, and wilted stunt. Management: Resistant varieties (Aruna, ADT 36, Co 42, Co 46, IR 36, IR 72); avoid close planting; provide 30 cm rogue spacing every 2.5 m; avoid excessive N; practice intermittent draining; use light traps and yellow pan traps; conserve predators (Lycosa pseudoannulata, Cyrtorhinus lividipennis); avoid synthetic pyrethroids, methyl parathion, fenthion, quinalphos; drain water before spray; apply Phosphamidon 40 SL @ 1000 ml/ha, Carbofuran 3 G @ 17.5 kg/ha, Imidacloprid 18.5 @ 100 ml/ha, Thiomethoxam 20 WDG @ 100 ml/ha, Dichlorvos 76 WSC @ 350 ml/ha, Neem oil 3% @ 15 L/ha, Iluppai oil 6% @ 30 L/ha, or NSKE 5% @ 25 kg/ha.

Damage symptoms: Sucks sap causing stunted growth and irregular patches of 'hopper burn'. Management: Avoid excessive nitrogenous fertilizers; control irrigation by intermittent draining; apply Phosphamidon 40 SL @ 1000 ml/ha, Carbofuran 3 G @ 17.5 kg/ha, Dichlorvos 76 WSC @ 350 ml/ha, Neem oil 3% @ 15 L/ha, Iluppai oil 6% @ 30 L/ha, or NSKE 5% @ 25 kg/ha.

Damage symptoms: Insects congregate in leaf sheaths sucking sap; plants become weak, yellowish, stunted in circular patches; white waxy fluff in leaf sheaths. Management: Remove grasses from bunds and trim bunds; destroy affected plants; spray Dimethoate 30 EC @ 500 ml/ha or Methyl demeton 25 EC @ 500 ml/ha; conserve natural enemies like Scymnus sp., Anatrichus pygmaeus, and Mepachymerus ensifer.

Damage symptoms: Sucking sap from grains at milky stage resulting in chaffy grains with black puncture spots; buggy odour in field. Management: Dust @ 25 kg/ha twice (at flowering and 1 week later) with Quinalphos 1.5 D, Carbaryl 10 D, Malathion 5 D, or KKM 10 D (10% Acorus calamus rhizome powder + 90% fly ash); or spray Fenthion 100 EC @ 500 ml/ha, Malathion 50 EC @ 500 ml/ha, NSKE 5% @ 25 kg/ha, or Notchi/Prosopis leaf extract 10% twice.

Symptoms: Infects all aerial parts at all stages. Leaf blast produces small specks enlarging to spindle-shaped spots (0.5-1.5 cm long, 0.3-0.5 cm wide) with ashy centers coalescing into irregular patches giving burnt appearance; severe cases cause lodging. Neck blast causes blackening, shriveling of neck region, inhibited grain set, and breaking of panicle. Nodal blast turns nodes black and causes them to break. Management: Avoid excess N, apply N in 3 splits, remove weed hosts on bunds; burn straw/stubble; grow tolerant varieties (Penna, Pinakini, Co 47, IR-64, etc.); dry seed treatment with Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 10 g/kg seed or Captan/Carbendazim/Thiram/Tricyclazole @ 2.0 g/kg; root soak seedlings in 2.5 kg P. fluorescens in 25 m2 water for 30 min; spray P. fluorescens 0.5% from 45 DAT at 10-day intervals (3 times); spray Tricyclazole @ 1 g/L or Edifenphos @ 1 ml/L or Carbendazim @ 1 g/L at nursery, tillering, and panicle emergence.

Symptoms: Seedling wilt or kresek; water-soaked to yellowish wavy stripes starting from leaf tips; milky or opaque bacterial ooze dewdrops on young lesions in morning; lesions turn yellow to white; cut ends of leaf make water turbid due to ooze. Management: Disease-free seeds; isolated upland nurseries; avoid seedling clipping; balanced fertilization, avoid excess N and skip N at booting if infected; drain field (except flowering); destroy wild hosts; avoid water flow from infected fields; grow tolerant varieties (IR 20, TKM 6); spray Streptomycin sulphate + Tetracycline combination 300 g + Copper oxychloride 1.25 kg/ha.

Symptoms: Stunting, reduced tillering, yellow or orange-yellow leaves with rust-colored spots starting from leaf tip down to leaf blade; delayed flowering; small, incompletely exerted panicles with mostly sterile or partially filled grains. Management: Light traps for vector monitoring; destroy weed hosts; spray 2% urea mixed with Mancozeb @ 2.5 g/L or 1% Multi-K (potassium nitrate); grow tolerant varieties (Co 45, Co 48, Surekha, Vikramarya, Bharani, IR 36); crop rotation with pulses/oilseeds; control green leafhopper vectors using Carbofuran 3 G @ 10 kg/acre (or 1 kg a.i./ha in nursery and tillering stage), or spray Fenthion/Phosphamidon @ 1.0 ml/L.

Symptoms: Initial water-soaked to greenish-gray lesions turning grayish-white with brown margins on leaf sheaths near waterline; presence of sclerotia; lesions coalesce causing death of whole leaf; partially filled or empty grains. Management: Apply FYM 12.5 t/ha or green manure 6.25 t/ha; soil application of P. fluorescens @ 2.5 kg/ha mixed with 50 kg FYM at 30 DAT; foliar spray P. fluorescens @ 0.2% at boot leaf stage and 10 days later; avoid irrigation water flow from infected fields; reduce N dose and skip top dressing; spray Carbendazim (1 g/L), Propiconazole (1 ml/L), Benomyl, Iprodione, Validamycin, or Polyoxin.

Symptoms: Irregular spots with dark reddish-brown margins and gray centers; flag leaf sheath discoloration; lesions coalesce covering sheath; young panicles remain enclosed in sheath; unemerged panicles rot and florets turn red-brown to dark brown; whitish powdery growth inside sheaths; sterile/shrivelled panicles. Management: Burn infected plant debris; apply Ipomea or Prosopis leaf powder extract 5% or NSKE 5%; spray Mancozeb @ 2.5 g/L, Carbendazim @ 1.0 g/L, or Benomyl @ 0.5 g/L at flowering stage.

Symptoms: Seedling blight in nursery and main field; isolated round to oval brown spots resembling sesame seeds (0.5 to 2.0 mm wide) coalescing into large patches; black/brown spots on glumes covered by olivaceous velvety growth; brown appearance on panicle neck; up to 50% yield reduction. Management: Use disease-free seeds; seed soak/treatment with Captan or Thiram @ 2.0 g/kg; spray Mancozeb (2.0 g/L) or Edifenphos (1 ml/L) 2-3 times at 10-15 day intervals during early hours or afternoon at flowering and post-flowering stages.

Symptoms: Individual rice grains transformed into a mass of yellow fruiting bodies; velvety spores enclose floral parts; immature spores are flattened, smooth, yellow, covered by membrane which ruptures as spores grow; mature spores become orange and turn yellowish-green or greenish-black. Management: Use disease-free seeds; destroy straw and stubble; spray Hexaconazole @ 1 ml/L or Chlorothalonil @ 2 g/L at tillering and pre-flowering stages.

Management: Spray Carbendazim + Mancozeb (1:1) @ 2 g/L at boot leaf stage and 50% flowering; store grains at 13-14% moisture.

Symptoms: Small, dark-green, water-soaked translucent streaks on veins from tillering to booting; lesions turn brown and bacteria ooze out under humid weather. Management: Secure disease-free seed; destroy wild collateral hosts; prevent water flow from affected fields; grow tolerant varieties (IR 20, TKM 6).

RSV isolates from eastern China and Yunnan are divided into two or three subtypes based on target genes. Pathogenicity of 23 RSV isolates collected from Yunnan, Jiangsu, Henan, and Anhui varies greatly when tested on rice cultivars Nihonbare and Hueyon 63.

Artificial inoculation at the seedling stage using RSV-viruliferous SBPHs infected 31 gramineous species, including rice, barley, wheat, oat, rye, maize, Italian rye-grass, perennial rye-grass, sudangrass, timothy, Setaria italica, Cyperus amuricus, Alopecurus aequalis, Digitaria adscendens, Echinochloa crus-galli, and Poa annua.

Infected plants show stunting, light green or yellow stripes on leaves, and a reduced number of tillers. Symptoms are more severe in rice, barley, wheat, maize, and Setaria italica, but milder in other species. Incubation period required for symptom development is longer in mildly infected weeds.

Nicotiana benthamiana seedlings mechanically inoculated with RSV-infected rice extracts develop chlorotic spots on inoculated leaves and systemic mosaic symptoms on newly developed leaves. Arabidopsis thaliana seedlings exposed to RSV-viruliferous SBPHs develop vein chlorosis on new leaves, stunting, distortion in flower stalks, and delayed onset of flowering.

Natural infection with RSV occurs in wheat and weed species including Setaria italica, Cynodon dactylon, Digitaria adscendens, Digitaria violascens, Eragrostis multicaulis, Panicum miliaceum, and Setaria viridis; however, weed hosts play a limited role in RS epidemics because infection occurs on rare occasions.

Mechanical inoculation of rice seedlings with RSV is not achieved, but seedlings can be infected at low rates by thrusting RS-infected rice extracts into vascular bundles of leaves using a syringe. SBPHs transmit RSV at low rates when fed for 2 days on 4-5 cm cuttings of rice sheaths previously incubated with RS-infected leaf extracts.
RSV is transmitted in a persistent manner by vector species including SBPH, Unkanodes sapporonus, and Unkanodes albifacia.

SBPH overwinters at the fourth instar as nymphal diapause at the basal part of winter cereals, weeds, or in soil cracks after moving to newly planted wheat, barley, or weeds in September or October. Overwintered adults appear in March or April and may move to early-planted rice fields or oviposit on winter cereals. First-generation nymphs appear in late April and develop into long-winged adults that migrate to newly transplanted rice fields in May to June. Second-generation adults appear around mid-June.

At Kamikawa in Hokkaido Region, Japan (about 44° north latitude), SBPH has two generations per year, and overwintered adults move directly to nursery beds or newly transplanted rice fields in mid-May to early June. After transplanting, SBPH populations gradually decrease in mid-August and then increase in mid-October.

Rice stripe symptoms appear in fields about one month after transplanting. Infected plants increase in number and reach maximum levels two months after transplanting. Infected seedlings easily wilt prematurely, and most symptomatic plants in the field are newly infected. Major infection is caused by first- and second-generation adults.

In northern Zhejiang, China, major RS infection occurs in June to early July by first-generation SBPHs in early-planted rice, and in late July by second-generation SBPHs at 15 to 25 days after transplanting, with limited infection occurring in mid- or late August likely by the third generation at the booting stage in late-planted rice.

RS incidence fluctuates depending on weather conditions, cropping practices, planting time, and cultivars. RS incidence is generally higher in areas with predominant winter cereal cropping, higher SBPH populations, and higher proportions of RSV carriers in overwintered populations. Regression analysis shows a linear relationship between SBPH density at the seedling stage and RS incidence.
RS incidence is high in plots transplanted earlier in late May, but lower in plots transplanted late in late June.
The relationship between yield reduction and RS disease incidence is linear, resulting in an average yield loss of 0.8% for every 1% increase in disease incidence.

In Jiangsu and Zhejiang, SBPH populations and RSV carrier percentages are monitored for the first generation in wheat fields and for the first and second generations in nursery beds for late rice. Two regression equations correlating percentage infected vectors with disease incidence are used to predict RS incidence. In Japan, overwintered SBPH density and RSV-carrier proportions have been monitored to forecast epidemics for timely insecticide applications.

Trap Barrier System (TBS): Erect 2 ft height polythene sheet barrier around the crop at 15 days after transplanting. Arrange a soil moat before the entry hole to facilitate the animal to enter easily inside the trap. Maintain water around the TBS and collect the successful traps every day and replace with new / emptied traps.

If the crop is submerged in water for more than 1 to 2 days in the boot leaf or flowering stage, panicle exertion may be incomplete. Water accumulation in the spikelets results in reduced fertilization and formation of chaffy seeds.
To avoid discoloration of grains during submergence, spray with Carbendiazim @ 1g/L or Carbendiazim + Mancozeb @ 2g/L or Propiconazole @ 1ml/L.

If the harvested sheaves in the field are drenched, 5% salt solution should be sprayed on the sheaves to prevent seed germination. The sheaves should be turned over, dried and threshed after cessation of the rains.

Grow green manure crops (Dhaincha, Sunhemp, Pillipesara and Cowpea) as preceding crop to Paddy and apply soil test-based fertilizers. The entire dose of phosphorus fertilizer should be applied during the final puddling stage.

Spraying of propiconazole @ 200ml/acre two times at booting stage and at 50% panicle emergence stage. At severe incidence of diseases spray tebuconazole + trifloxystrobin 75WG @ 80g/acre.

Affected stubbles are to be destroyed by burning or through ploughing; judicious use of nitrogenous fertilizers; avoid clipping of tip of seedling at the time of transplanting; avoid flooded conditions or drying of the field (not at the time of flowering); application of potassium two times @ 15 kg/acre at planting time and 20 kg/acre at panicle initiation stage.

Straw Baling Machine is used to bundle paddy straw into either round or square/rectangular shapes for easy handling and transport.

During nursery seed bed preparation, well decomposed FYM should be applied 2-3 days before sowing @ 10 q/ 1000 m² or vermicompost can be used @ 500kg/1000 sq.m and Azospirillum may be applied @ 2 kg /1000 sq.m area. 1000 sq.m nursery area is sufficient for transplanting of one hectare land.
Clipping of leaf tips during transplanting to remove egg masses laid by stem borer; Release of Trichogramma @50000/ha for 4 times to control stem borer.
Formation of alleyways during transplanting (20cm); and application of Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 20 g/m² at the time of sowing are the common plant protection measure to be followed.
First ploughing should be given at least 21 days before transplanting. 2nd ploughing at 10-12 days before transplanting and final puddling should be done 4-5 days before transplanting.

The rice transplanting for mid and high altitude should be completed by month of June and in low altitude it should be completed by first fortnight of July. Transplanting should be done with 3 seedlings per hill. Spacings should be 20 × 15 cm (33 hills /sq.m) for semi-dwarf and 20 × 20 cm (25 hills/sq.m) for tall traditional varieties.

Maintain 25 hills/sq.m for tall traditional varieties.

Land is thoroughly puddled and seedbeds of 10 m length and 1.25 m breadth are prepared with a 30 cm gap in between the beds. The length of the bed may vary according to convenience.
In each seedbed, apply 20-30 kg cow dung/compost, 80 g urea, 80 g SSP, and 40 g MOP, and mix well with the soil.
Well germinated seeds are to be sown @ 650 g to 1 kg per bed depending on grain size. Requirement of seed for transplanting one hectare of main field is 40-45 kg.

Irrigation water should be applied in furrows to maintain saturated conditions in the surface soil of the nursery bed. Standing water to a depth of 2-3 cm should be maintained at least 2-3 days before uprooting.
As soon as one or two blast spots are seen in the nursery, ediphenphos @ 1 ml/l of water is to be sprayed.
For management of root knot nematode in the nursery, apply Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 20 g/sq. m at the time of sowing.

Apply well rotten FYM or compost @ 10 t/ha during field preparation.

Give two weedings with a paddy weeder or hoe at 20 and 40 days after transplanting.

Soil fertility can be enhanced by incorporating Dhaincha (Sesbania aculeata) as a green manure 60-70 days pre-transplanting, ploughed under 15-20 days before transplanting.

Manage yellow stem borer (Tryporyza incertulus) and leaf folder (Cnaphalocrocis medinalis) by clipping terminal shoots prior to transplanting, followed by application of Cartap Hydrochloride @ 2.0 g/L of water. Cleaning of the field and bund management should be done before the monsoon, and summer ploughing should be done which helps to destroy pathogens and weed seeds.
Paddy should be sown in line and pre-emergence herbicide should be sprayed three days after sowing, such as Pretilachlor 50% EC @ 1500 ml/ha or Pyrazosulfuron 10% WP @ 200 ml/ha.

Farmers are advised to get their soil tested by contacting the local agricultural officer or nearby Krishi Vigyan Kendra. Based on the soil test results, balanced fertilizers should be applied accordingly.
Paddy seeds should be treated with a 17% salt solution before raising the nursery or direct seeding.

Use the recommended seed rate: for line sowing, 80-90 kg/ha; for the Biasi and broadcast methods, 100-120 kg/ha. For the transplanting method, prepare the nursery in approximately 1/10 of the total field area. Use 50 kg/ha of seed for thick-grained varieties and 40 kg/ha for thin-grained varieties.

Follow herbicide application within 3 days after sowing with a post emergence application of Bispyribac sodium (10%) @ 250 ml/ha.
If symptoms of sheath blight disease are observed in paddy field, spray Hexaconazole @ 1000 ml/ha.
